> **The research decision.** Your analysis printed a number. Now you decide the
> sentence that number lets you assert: the headline you will show in public and
> defend out loud, worded so its verb stays inside what your design established and
> its uncertainty rides in the same eye-span. You choose the words. You lock them.
> You never let a tool talk your claim past its boundary.

## Why this decision matters

**The decision on the table: the verb in your headline, and how far your evidence
lets it reach.**

> *"In the poster hall I point at one number and ask where it came from and what it
> lets you say. If the headline reads 'lowers blood pressure' but the study only
> watched who chose to walk, I stop reading. A claim that outruns its evidence tells
> me to distrust the whole board."*
> — a **research-integrity judge** working a poster session

A result is not yet a claim. Your analysis prints a number; your headline asserts a
sentence. The gap between them is where most projects break, because the sentence
almost always wants to say more than the number earned. The judge above is not
testing your statistics. She is testing whether your words match the evidence
underneath them. This chapter is the habit that closes that gap before a stranger
finds it open.

## The concept

Start with the two words this chapter lives between. A **result** is a number your
analysis produced, such as a difference of 6 points between two group averages. A
**claim** is a sentence you assert and will defend, such as "the walking group had
lower blood pressure." Turning the first into the second is a decision, not a
formatting step, because you choose how much the sentence is allowed to say.

Four ideas govern that choice, and keeping the first three apart is what stops
overclaiming before it starts.

Your **question** is what you set out to learn, and its kind comes from its own
words. Example: "does walking lower blood pressure?" asks what an intervention
would change, so it is causal, and it stays causal no matter which data you
managed to collect.

Your **identification status** is whether this design can actually deliver that
answer [@blair2023rdss]. Example: if you watched who already chose to walk, nothing separates the
walking from the kind of person who walks, so your status is *not identified by this
design under the assumptions I can defend*. Notice what that status does not say. It
never repeats the word "causal", because the kind belongs to the question and the
status belongs to the design; writing "causal and unidentified" as one status quietly
fuses the two fields you just separated.

Your **result** is the quantity this evidence did produce. Here that is a
descriptive association between walking and blood pressure, which is real and worth
reporting, and which sits beside the causal question rather than replacing it.

Written out, the four fields make a card you can reuse on any project:

> **Question kind:** causal.
> **Identification status:** not identified by this design under stated assumptions.
> **Result:** observed association.
> **Claim boundary:** association only.

Your **claim boundary** is what those three together license you to write, and it
lives in the headline verb. Example: with no identification argument, you write "was
associated with lower," never "lowered." Read the condition carefully: what earns a
causal verb is a defended identification argument [@hernan2020whatif]. Randomizing is the cleanest way
to get one, and the observational-causal pathway earlier in the book shows designs that carry causal
answers when their assumptions are argued and defended. What you may never do is
use the verb without the argument.

![Three fields kept apart, and the verb they license between them. The kind belongs to the question and the status belongs to the
design.](../images/concepts/claim_boundary_verb.png){fig-alt="Three boxes side by side: question kind, what you set out to learn, here causal;
identification status, whether this design can actually deliver that answer, here not identified by this design under stated assumptions; and result,
the quantity this evidence did produce, here an observed association. Arrows from all three converge on a box labelled claim boundary, what those
three together license you to write. Beneath it, two headline verbs: you write was associated with lower; never lowered, which is struck through."}

One more idea makes the claim's honesty visible. **Uncertainty in the
same eye-span** means the interval or caveat sits right beside the claim, not in a
footnote [@wasserstein2016asa]. Example: "about 6 points lower (95% interval: 1 to 11)" printed under the
headline, so a reader meets the doubt at the same moment as the number. The numbers
in this chapter's examples are constructed to make the point; the uncertainty lesson you already worked through builds
intervals properly. A bound a
reader has to hunt for is a bound doing hidden work.

One more habit backs all of this. **Traceability** means every number you show walks
back to the exact notebook cell that produced it. Example: the 6-point gap on your
board points to the one line of code that computed it, and you can show that line
when a judge asks. A number you cannot trace cannot go up.

## A worked example

A biology student runs a small human-physiology pilot. Forty volunteers wear a
step tracker for a month. Twenty walk at least 8,000 steps a day; twenty do not.
Their average resting systolic blood pressure comes out at 128 in the active group
and 134 in the less-active group, a 6-point gap.

The result is that 6-point gap. The claim is the decision. The draft headline reads
"Walking LOWERS blood pressure," drawn as two bars on an axis that starts at 125,
which makes the small gap look like a cliff, with the two groups told apart by red
and green alone.

Walk the decision. The question behind this study is causal, and it stays causal:
you want to know whether walking lowers blood pressure. What the design cannot do is
answer it. Nobody was assigned to walk, so the active group may differ in age, diet,
or baseline health, and the comparison leaves that untouched. Fill the card: question
kind causal, identification status not identified by this design, result an observed
association. Those three together fix what the claim may say. The verb
"lowers" claims a crossing the design never paid for, and the honest verb is "was
associated with lower." The truncated axis is the next problem: bars encode
magnitude, so starting them at 125 makes a 6-point gap look like a cliff. Start the
bars at a meaningful zero, or better, plot the two group averages as points with
their intervals on a blood-pressure scale a clinician would recognize. The interval
reported here runs roughly 1 to 11 points (constructed for the example), wide enough
that the honest headline must carry it in the
same eye-span. And each bar gets a direct value label, so a color-blind or
screen-reader reader receives the number, not just the hue.

The locked claim: "In this sample, more-active volunteers averaged about 6 points
lower resting systolic blood pressure (95% interval: 1 to 11); this is an observed
association, and this design does not identify whether walking caused the drop." Same result, a claim that
survives the judge.

What licenses a causal verb is the identification argument, not the size of the gap you observed [@hernan2020whatif].

The block below builds the forty volunteers and prints the gap along with one thing the poster never showed: how the two groups differ before you compare them.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# Forty volunteers who CHOSE how much they walk. Age drives both.
n = 40
age = np.r_[rng.normal(31, 7, 20), rng.normal(43, 7, 20)]   # active are younger
active = np.r_[np.ones(20, bool), np.zeros(20, bool)]
systolic = np.round(112 + 0.5 * age + rng.normal(0, 6, n))

gap = systolic[~active].mean() - systolic[active].mean()
print(f"active group mean systolic      : {systolic[active].mean():.0f}")
print(f"less-active group mean systolic : {systolic[~active].mean():.0f}")
print(f"observed gap                    : {gap:.0f} points")
print(f"mean age, active vs less-active : {age[active].mean():.0f} vs "
      f"{age[~active].mean():.0f}")
print("\nnobody was assigned to walk. the age line is one difference you can")
print("see; the design leaves every unseen one untouched, so the verb stays")
print("'is associated with'")
```

## Who it works for and why

Suppose you later run the walking study properly. Two hundred
adults enroll, a coin decides who joins a walking program, and everyone's resting
blood pressure is measured at the end. The coin gives you the identification
argument the pilot lacked, so the overall headline may now carry a causal verb.
The next question arrives fast: does it work for
everyone, and how does it work? Those are two questions, and each has its own trap.

**Effect heterogeneity** is the idea that a treatment can change an outcome by
different amounts for different kinds of people. Example: a walking program might
lower blood pressure more in older adults, whose pressure starts higher, than in
twenty-year-olds. A **moderator** is a trait, measured before treatment, that marks
those groups, such as age, sex, or starting blood pressure. The same question turns
up in every field. An economist asks whether a job-training program raises earnings
more for workers without a degree; a plant biologist asks whether a fertilizer helps
a crop more on poor soil.

Two rules keep a subgroup claim inside its evidence. The first is timing. A
**pre-specified moderator** is one you named in your declared design, with the
reason you expect it to matter, before any outcome was measured. Example: "we
expect a larger effect among adults over 50, because their pressure starts
higher." Cut the sample twenty ways after the fact and, by chance alone, one slice
will probably look special. That slice is a lead for your next study, labeled exploratory in
this one. Naming moderators in advance does not cure the arithmetic by itself: declare
twenty and the same luck is waiting in one of them. Keep the list short, report how many
differences you examined, and read any single striking one against that count.

The second rule is to test the difference, not the two labels. A result is usually called
**statistically significant** when its 95% interval leaves out zero. A common slip reads
one subgroup's estimate as "significant," the other's as "not significant," and
concludes that the program works for one group and fails for the other. Gelman and
Stern showed why that reasoning breaks: the gap between a significant result and a
non-significant one need not itself be significant, or even large
[@gelman2006difference]. A claim that the effect differs is a claim about one
number, the difference between the two subgroup effects, and that number needs its
own interval.

The block below builds a trial where the truth is simple: walking lowers systolic
pressure by exactly 5 points in younger and older adults alike. Watch what the two
subgroup estimates suggest, then read the last line.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# A randomized walking program. 140 younger and 60 older adults.
# The TRUE effect is the SAME in both groups: 5 points lower systolic.
younger = np.r_[np.ones(140, bool), np.zeros(60, bool)]
walk = rng.permutation(np.r_[np.ones(100, bool), np.zeros(100, bool)])
systolic = 125 + 12 * ~younger - 5 * walk + rng.normal(0, 12, 200)

def gap(mask):
    a, b = systolic[mask & walk], systolic[mask & ~walk]
    est = a.mean() - b.mean()
    se = np.sqrt(a.var(ddof=1) / len(a) + b.var(ddof=1) / len(b))
    return est, se

for name, mask in [("younger", younger), ("older", ~younger)]:
    est, se = gap(mask)
    print(f"{name:<8} effect estimate : {est:+.1f}  (95% interval {est-1.96*se:+.1f} to {est+1.96*se:+.1f})")
(ey, sy), (eo, so) = gap(younger), gap(~younger)
d, sd = eo - ey, np.sqrt(sy**2 + so**2)
print(f"difference, older minus younger : {d:+.1f}  (95% interval {d-1.96*sd:+.1f} to {d+1.96*sd:+.1f})")
print("\nthe truth is the same 5 points in both groups. the older group only")
print("looks twice as helped; read the difference line before you say so")
```

Among younger adults, walkers ended about 4 points below non-walkers (95% interval:
0.2 to 8.0); among older adults, about 10 points below (95% interval: 4.0 to 16.6). A draft headline would
say the program works more than twice as well after fifty. The difference line
disagrees: about 6 points, with an interval running from 13.6 points more benefit
for older adults to 1.2 points more for younger ones. That interval includes zero,
and you built this world so that the true difference is exactly zero. Sixty older
adults split across two arms is a small sample. The claim the evidence licenses is: "we found no clear evidence that the
effect differs by age (estimated difference: about 6 points more benefit for older
adults, 95% interval from 13.6 points more to 1.2 points less)." Read that interval
in both directions. It leaves room for no difference, and it also leaves room for a
large one, so it is not evidence that the effect is the same for everyone either.
Even a clear difference would have a limit. The coin assigned walking, never age,
so a subgroup gap tells you where the effect is larger without telling you that age
is the reason. Older adults also differ in weight, medication, and starting pressure.

The *why* question asks about a **mechanism**, the chain of steps through which a
treatment changes an outcome. Example: walking might lower blood pressure partly
through weight loss and partly through changes in the blood vessels themselves. A
**mediator** is a variable on that chain, measured after treatment, such as body
weight at the end of the program. The tempting analysis measures weight and reports
how much of the effect "goes through" it. Imai, Keele, Tingley, and Yamamoto show
that this split rests on an assumption the data cannot test, which they call
sequential ignorability, and that randomizing the treatment secures only its first half
[@imai2011unpacking]. The second half says that, among people with the same treatment and
the same background traits, weight is as good as randomly assigned. Nobody randomized the weight
loss, so anything that drives both weight and pressure, such as a change in diet
during the program, contaminates the split, and that holds even when the program itself
caused the diet change. Their answer is a sensitivity analysis that asks how large a
violation would have to be to erase the estimated indirect effect. Bullock, Green, and Ha reach the same
verdict for psychology experiments: learning about a mediator usually takes a
program of experiments built for that purpose [@bullock2010yes]. The defensible
default is to report the overall effect with its causal verb, and the program's effect
on weight with one too, since the coin assigned that comparison as well ("walkers ended
the program lighter than the comparison group"). What the coin never assigned is weight
itself, so the link from weight to pressure, and the share of the effect that runs
through it, becomes a hypothesis your next design could test. Each of those sentences fills
the same four-field card you used above; the mechanism sentence carries a
status of *not identified by this design*.

A tool does the arithmetic here well. It will fit a model that lets the effect
differ by group, compute the interval for a difference, and list moderators that other studies examined (each one
a claim you check in the source). Its failure is just as predictable. Ask "who does
the program work for?" and it will slice the data every way the columns allow, then
return the slices that cleared a threshold, each with a fluent explanation attached.
That is the twenty-slices trap run at machine speed. Your pre-specified list is the
defense: the tool computes on the moderators you named, and anything else it finds
goes under an exploratory label. Which moderators matter, and which mechanism you are
willing to claim, stay your decisions.

When your question is how a process unfolds rather than how large an effect is,
the [qualitative inquiry route](../part7-further-routes/qualitative-inquiry.qmd)
traces mechanisms through what people did and said, and the observational-causal
pathway earlier in the book shows process tracing inside a single case.

## Claims that travel

Now picture a second, larger walking trial: 400 volunteers on a campus, randomized
the same way, and only about one in six of them over fifty. A public-health officer
in a nearby retirement community reads
your poster and asks the question every good result eventually meets: will this
work for my residents? Your interval answers a question about the people you
studied. Hers is about people you never enrolled. The number she wants is the
average effect among her residents, a different estimand from the average effect
among your volunteers. On the inquiry compass her question keeps its causal kind
but moves its reach to a new setting, the cell the compass calls a transported effect.
The coin licensed the causal claim for your volunteers; the crossing to her residents
needs a license of its own, a transport argument, because random sampling from her
community is one you do not have.

**External validity** is the extent to which a result from the people, treatment,
outcome, and setting you studied holds for the ones someone else cares about.
Findley, Kikuta, and Denly note that researchers invoke it constantly and rarely
argue for it, and they recommend that studies report a routine discussion of it
[@findley2021external]. Egami and Hartman split the question into four parts, one
for each thing that can change between study and target: the population, the
treatment, the outcome, and the context [@egami2023elements]. Example, in your own
trial: campus volunteers versus retirees (population), a supervised program versus
a leaflet telling people to walk (treatment), pressure taken by a nurse versus a
home cuff (outcome), and a walkable campus versus a suburb with no sidewalks
(context). The other domains face the same four checks. A microfinance evaluation
in one country, a get-out-the-vote experiment in one city, and a drought-tolerance
result from a greenhouse all have to argue their way to the next country, city, or
field.

Randomization does not settle any of this. It makes the comparison fair inside the
trial, and that is all it promises. Deaton and Cartwright put it plainly: a trial's
estimate applies to the sample that was in it, and carrying it to any other group
needs its own justification [@deaton2018understanding].

Two terms make that justification concrete. Your **target population** is the group
you want your claim to speak about, named before you argue. Example: residents of
one retirement community, most of them over seventy. **Transport** means carrying an
estimate from the population you studied to a target population by reasoning about
what differs between them. Moderators from the previous section whose mix differs between your sample and the
target are what make transport hard. If the effect is larger for older adults, and the target is mostly
older adults, the trial's overall average is the wrong number for them.

When the difference that matters is one you measured, you can reweight.
**Reweighting** means recomputing the average so each group counts in proportion to
its share of the target rather than its share of your sample. Example: if older
adults are 17 percent of your volunteers but 70 percent of the residents, the older
adults' effect gets a weight of 0.7. The block
below builds a trial where the effect really does depend on age (3 points for
younger adults, 9 for older ones), then recomputes the average as if seventy percent
of the volunteers had been older, which is the target's age mix.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# A randomized walking trial run on a campus: about 80% younger adults.
# In this constructed world the TRUE effect differs by age:
# 3 points lower for younger adults, 9 points lower for older adults.
n = 400
older = rng.random(n) < 0.20
walk = rng.permutation(np.r_[np.ones(n // 2, bool), np.zeros(n // 2, bool)])
systolic = 122 + 14 * older - np.where(older, 9, 3) * walk + rng.normal(0, 12, n)
df = pd.DataFrame({"older": older, "walk": walk, "sbp": systolic})

def effect(d):
    a, b = d.sbp[d.walk], d.sbp[~d.walk]
    return a.mean() - b.mean(), a.var(ddof=1) / len(a) + b.var(ddof=1) / len(b)

(e_all, v_all) = effect(df)
(e_y, v_y), (e_o, v_o) = effect(df[~df.older]), effect(df[df.older])
share_old = 0.70          # the retirement community you want to speak about
e_t = (1 - share_old) * e_y + share_old * e_o
se_t = np.sqrt((1 - share_old) ** 2 * v_y + share_old ** 2 * v_o)
print(f"older adults in the trial         : {older.mean():.0%}")
print(f"trial average effect              : {e_all:+.1f}  (95% interval {e_all-1.96*np.sqrt(v_all):+.1f} to {e_all+1.96*np.sqrt(v_all):+.1f})")
print(f"reweighted to a 70%-older target  : {e_t:+.1f}  (95% interval {e_t-1.96*se_t:+.1f} to {e_t+1.96*se_t:+.1f})")
print(f"true effect in that target        : {-(0.3*3 + 0.7*9):+.1f}")
print("\nreweighting fixes the age mix you measured. it cannot fix a")
print("difference between campus and community that you never measured")
```

Seventeen percent of the volunteers were older, and the trial's average effect is
about 2.8 points lower (95% interval: 0.4 to 5.3). Reweighted to the community's age
mix, the estimate becomes about 5.1 points lower (95% interval: 0.8 to 9.5), closer to
the 7.2 points you planted for that target. Notice the price. The interval grew from about 5
points wide to about 9, because the transported number leans hard on the roughly
seventy older volunteers. And the interval still treats the target's 70 percent as known exactly. The whole
calculation also rests on two assumptions. First, among people in the same age group,
the effect on campus equals the effect in the community, so any other trait that changes
the effect must be spread the same way in both places. Second, the trial held enough
people of every kind the target contains to learn their effect at all. The first
assumption hides a further one.
Your "older" volunteers on a campus are likely in their fifties and sixties, and
the residents are mostly past seventy, so the calculation also assumes a volunteer of fifty-five
stands in for a resident of seventy-five. If the retirees also take blood-pressure
medication or live without sidewalks, no reweighting of age repairs that. You argue
it from what is known about those differences, or you narrow the claim.

That narrowing has a home on the card. Add a scope line under the claim boundary:
"Scope: adults like these volunteers, in a setting like this campus; transport to
older or less mobile groups assumes that, within an age group, nothing that changes the
effect differs between campus and community." A reader can
now see where your claim stops traveling, instead of discovering it later.

AI tools generalize by default. Ask one to summarize your trial and it writes
"walking lowers blood pressure in adults," dropping the campus, the age mix, and
the supervised program in one fluent sentence. That is a **silent scope change**
aimed at the population rather than the verb. A tool is useful on the other side
of the problem: it can list ways a target setting might differ from yours and draft
the reweighting code. Each difference it lists is a claim to check against a real
source, and choosing the target, and judging whether the unmeasured differences are
small enough to defend, stays with you.

When several studies of the same question exist in different places, comparing
their results is some of the most direct evidence you will get about whether an effect
travels, though studies run in different places usually differ in design too. The [evidence synthesis route](../part7-further-routes/evidence-synthesis.qmd)
shows how to gather those studies and read how much they disagree.

## An AI failure case

You paste your honest headline into a tool and ask it to make it "punchier." It
returns, with total confidence, "Walking Reduces Blood Pressure by 6 Points." It
reads beautifully and it is wrong. The tool upgraded your verb from an association
to a cause and dropped your interval, a silent scope change dressed up as a copy
edit.

You catch it by comparing the new verb to what your design earned. Your question was
causal and stays causal, but nobody was assigned to walk, so nothing identifies that
answer and "reduces" claims a warrant you never held. You
also notice the "6 points" now stands alone with no interval beside it. You revert
to "was associated with about 6 points lower (95% interval: 1 to 11)." The fluent
rewrite reviewed your style; only you can review your claim.

*After the last chapter you know where your confidence actually stops; this step
turns each of your results into a sentence you would print and defend.*

The hands-on half of this section lives in the chapter's **companion notebook**: open it in Colab with the badge at the top, and work the steps there.

Commit your own answer first, then delegate. Each prompt is a checkable job, never
a request for a verdict.

Expect to run each one more than once. You read what comes back, name the part that
is wrong, and ask again with that correction in the prompt. That back-and-forth is
the method, not a sign you prompted badly. Some tools now run several rounds on
their own before showing you anything, which raises the stakes on your last step
rather than lowering them, because more of the reasoning happened where you could
not watch it.

::: {.callout-important title="Do not delegate"}
Three calls stay yours. You choose the **verb in your headline**, the one word that
fixes your claim boundary. You make the **defend-or-concede call** when a question
pushes on that boundary out loud. And you make the **lock decision**: the judgment
that every number is traced, every citation resolves, and the claim is ready to be
final. A tool can draft questions and hunt sources, but it cannot decide what your
evidence licenses or when your claim is earned.
:::

1. List every result you might put in front of a reader, then write the claim
   sentence each one licenses.
2. Check every verb against what your design established, and downgrade the ones
   that reach too far. "Caused" becomes "was associated with"; "predicts" becomes
   "flagged."

   **Red-team the verb.**

   ```text
   Here is my written headline: "[paste it]." Act as a hostile reviewer and find every
   place the verb claims more than an observational design licenses. Do not rewrite it
   for me; list the exact words so I can fix them myself.
   ```

   After running, verify: read each flagged word against your compass position and keep
   only the objections your design actually forces. Counters *silent scope change* (a
   claim quietly upgraded from association to cause).
3. Write a boundary line beside each claim naming what it does not establish, and
   put the uncertainty in the same eye-span as the number.

   **Turn your result into a checklist of hard questions.**

   ```text
   Here is my headline claim: "[paste it]". My question is causal, my design is
   observational and does not identify it, and what I actually estimated is a
   descriptive association. Generate the eight hardest questions a skeptic would ask,
   and mark which single audit each one belongs to: claim boundary, figure honesty,
   uncertainty, or accessibility.
   ```

   After running, verify: map every question to an audit and check it against your
   printed numbers; a missing audit is a gap the tidy list hid. Counters *illusion of
   completeness* (a long, organized list that skips the one flaw that matters most).
4. Trace every number back to the cell that produced it and cut the ones you cannot
   walk back. Then pick your lead claim, the sentence you would say first if you had
   ten seconds.
5. Log it in your AI Research Ledger, and verify at least one claim with a named
   method from the [Verification Guide](../verification-guide.qmd). An AI reviewer
   may run the check with you; the decision to accept or reject stays yours.

   **Locate the real source behind a physiology claim.**

   ```text
   Act as a literature assistant in human physiology. My headline claims regular
   walking is linked to lower blood pressure. Name up to three peer-reviewed sources
   or clinical guidelines that support this, with title, authors, year, and venue.
   Only list work you are confident exists; mark anything uncertain.
   ```

   After running, verify: open each source in a library database and confirm it exists
   and says what you claim. Counters *confident fabrication* (an invented citation
   arrives as confidently as a real one).
